utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, to my learned colleagues from the Defence, General Delic, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis and Matthias Neuner for the Prosecution, assisted by Alma Imamovic, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to my colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor, and everyone in and around the courtroom. I'm Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for the Defence of General Delic, with our assistant, Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And good morning to you, Mr. Loncaric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You deserve a special greeting. Just to remind you that you made a declaration at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. You are still bound by that declaration. Okay. All right, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Yesterday, we stopped at the point when we were talking about the book of rules of acknowledgments, you will remember. I want to pull the book of rules up again on the screen, and this time we are choosing the Exhibit D978, which is identical to PT6291 which was presented yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say Exhibit D978?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, PT -- D978.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We see here the page from the RBiH gazette and the rules of acknowledge, and I'm interested in Article 2, we talked yesterday already about it. The first sentence, and you told us something about the reasons when units were awarded. I want to move on to the second sentence now and read it to you. It says: "In extraordinary cases, acknowledgments may also be awarded to foreign citizens, foreign international bodies and organisations." My question to you is: Could you explain what are reasons which constitute extraordinary cases?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extraordinary citations could be awarded to anyone who assisted in a defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, either materially or in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand. What I'm trying to find out is we're talking here in this second sentence about awards to foreigners. What are extraordinary -- what were extraordinary cases at the time, according to which awards were granted?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those -- the circumstances and the criteria were determined by the proposer, and in the proposal they would say why -- state why they were proposing this individual or unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Now, we will later on see maybe one or two such proposals. I want to move on to Exhibit 111 which was shown to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want to do with PT978?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Since the witness also commented upon the first sentence yesterday and this morning on the second sentence, I would ask that it be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Just a second, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your microphone is on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit number 1375.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: May I have Exhibit 111 being shown, please. While it is coming up, I can introduce it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You have seen it yesterday already. It is, as you can see, a document from the 3rd Corps, from the 10th of November, 1995, and you said -- you will remember that there was some handwriting on certain pages of this document, and you said, therefore, that it was a draft only. And I understood you also to mean that you did not obtain such a document because it was type-signed, this version. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I just want you for a moment to look at this reference number on the top left corner. I'm referring to 04/15-114. Please remember that number. And I want now to show you another version of that document, which is signed, and that's PT6290. If we could scroll in maybe on the top part for a moment so that the witness can see the reference number and the date. Do you see that this has the same reference number, 04/15-114?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And it's also the same date as the previous document, 10th of November, 1995? Could you confirm that, please?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If we could for a moment go to the last page to show the signature to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this signature?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmuljin's.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If we look for a moment at the addressee here to the left-hand side, and in English we need to go to the last page, actually, it says here: "Delivered to." And if you look at the second hyphen, please, it says here: "Delivered to the Main Staff of the ARBiH Army Administration for Personnel and Legal Affairs." Do you remember that you have received this document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So, in fact -- I withdraw that. Could we go to the first page again now, please, and I'm referring here to the section C(1). It is proposed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but for the record I would like to mention the documents, the English and the Bosnian version of this document, P6290, do not correspond, because in the Bosnian version there is no key that is mentioned in the English version, nor the explanation of what the acronyms mean. Your Honour, in the BiH Army -- if we can now see the last page briefly. This was the reason why I stood up, because the last page is no longer on the screen. So the last page of both the Bosnian and English versions. Now, if you look at the English version, it says "Legend" or "Key," and then there is a whole list that does not exist in the document in the Bosnian language. And, Your Honour, I would like to mention something in regard to this key. The Yugoslav People's Army, as well as the BH Army, had regulated what acronyms stand for, so the Translation Service cannot just do it on their own and interpret these acronyms. In addition, this is not part of this document, and I would request that it be struck from this document because it does not exist in the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I can say I thank my learned colleague for this remark, because two days ago, when I tried to get a translation done, I noticed the same, that here indeed is a legend, and I, in fact, spoke to the translator herself about this fact, that here is a legend. I can explain what I have learned on that occasion. This document here is basically, apart from the signature and the missing handwritings, the same as the Exhibit 111, and the translation relating to Exhibit 111 also carries this legend. So I was speaking to the translator about the fact why is here a legend and why is Exhibit 111 or the translation of it a legend, and I was informed by the translator that there are a lot of abbreviation used in this lengthy proposal by the 3rd Corps, and as far as I understand it, the Translation Service, which is doing on a day-to-day basis translations, they understand what these abbreviations mean, and in order to provide a full translation of it, they are attaching here this type of legend to it. This is the explanation which I was given. I don't, from the Prosecution side, have any further remark to this. I cannot assess it. This is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you say what you want to say, Madam Vidovic, is this legend there in the B/C/S version of Exhibit 111?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It is not there, and that's why I actually approached the translator and said to the translator, "Shouldn't it be taken out," but I got the response I just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first I would like to say that Exhibit 111 and these exhibit are not identical. One part of the document only is identical. That's the first thing I wanted to say. As for the key, it does not exist in the original, in the Bosnian version, it isn't there. And secondly, Your Honour, in another case we had a major issue about this, and we discussed this with the Prosecutor, as to what these acronyms mean, and it turned out that their translators translated these acronyms rather freely. In other words, this does not correspond to the official acronyms that were used either in the BH Army or the former JNA. And even if they were in this document, even if the key was in this document, we would not accept the translation of it. And I don't believe -- I mean, last week we had an issue about a single sentence, a single word, that was crossed out, and here we have a whole page, almost, of explanations added in the English version that doesn't exist at all in the Bosnian version. And I would appreciate for you to order the Prosecutor to strike this legend or this key from the document, because it doesn't exist in the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all due respect, I think perhaps the simplest solution is simply for the Chamber to send a memo to CLSS and ask them to explain that. I believe this has come up in a number of cases. CLSS has a glossary of military terms. CLSS does not work for the Office of the Prosecutor, they are part of the Registry, they are the official translation service. If they put something on a document, we submit it based on what CLSS or the translation services do. It's a relatively simple process to get clarification as to why certain abbreviations are put on documents and abbreviations are used within documents, and I think that would certainly be the simplest solution.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may reply. The document, the Bosnian version, the original, has -- the translation has to be true to the original. This key does not exist in the original. What the Prosecutor can do is to provide to Your Honours a list of acronyms, or perhaps a document with acronyms, and then the Defence will reply to that and say whether it accepts that list or not. So it is not up to the Translation Service to interpret documents or translate them. We can sit down with the Prosecution and agree on what these acronyms mean. But adding something that is not in the document, that is unacceptable. I also claim that this is not the practice so far, because we had a similar situation in the Oric case, and the Trial Chamber ordered the parties to sit down and agree on what the acronyms mean, and it ordered the Prosecutor to provide a list to which the Defence will provide an answer. Following that, the Defence provided an official list of acronyms. And believe me, Your Honours, it differed significantly from the acronyms and the translation of the acronyms provided from the Translation Service. They cannot interpret and add onto documents what was not in the original, and I think that is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I simply need to note that within CLSS there is the reference terminology and document processing unit, a specialised department within CLSS which, among other things, maintains the official terminology database and compiles glossaries for use of language staff, and manages CLSS's library of reference materials, and I would be very low to be in a situation where the parties are agreeing upon acronyms when, in fact, the official translation service has a unit within it that is the official compiler and maintainer of this type of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just looking at this briefly, cursorily, looking at this key, I can tell you that it is completely mis-translated. For instance, there is an acronym "DKoV."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've told us that already. The Prosecution is ordered to strike off this legend. The Chamber will make no order as to future conduct on legends. If the parties want to agree, it's up to you to agree, and you can contact CLSS on your own and make sure that what you agree upon is agreeable also to what CLSS does. But to the extent that there is no legend on the B/C/S version of this document, the Chamber orders that the legend on the English be struck off. You may proceed, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, I want to go back to the first page, where we were a moment ago, yes, and I asked you, before that intervention from my learned colleague, whether you could please look at letter C. If we could scroll down in English, please. Yes. It says here -- Mr. Mahmuljin says: "We propose that ..." And number C: " ... written commendations be granted to the following units of the RBiH Army." And then you see, under number 1, the El Mujahedin Detachment headed by Abu Maali. Do you remember this request or that instance that you received this request or this proposal?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of this proposal, and I actually processed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I just want to point out the second person which is also mentioned in the proposal, and this is in section J of it. We need to go for a moment in B/C/S to page 4 and English to page 5, please. I think the English is not right. I need section J. In English, I said "page 5," and I see it's "page 4" in English. This is just to show you the heading, and I think we need to scroll up a little bit. I'm sorry, then it must be maybe 6 in English. I need section J. 7, thank you. It says here -- I just need the heading for a moment: "Written Commendations." You find that also. And now I need to go to number 72, which is, in B/C/S, on page 5, and in English, I believe at the second-last page, penultimate page. So written commendation is proposed here for Abu El Maali, as we can see from the El Mujahedin Detachment under number 72. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the whole order. But individually, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With the entire explanations given about that document, I would ask that it be admitted into evidence as a refreshing example, especially since the witness could yesterday not remember that this document had been received by him, and today he has said it repeatedly, and he said that even he has processed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first a reply to this last comment. The witness did not see this document yesterday. He saw document E111, which is at least five times as long as this document and it is different. And he said that this was the draft document, so it is not the same document. Now, this document here has to do with the establishment of the guilt of the accused, so it is not a refreshing exercise. The witness accepted the contents, so it has nothing to do with the credibility of the witness and exploring that aspect. He said yesterday that the El Mujahedin Detachment did get this citations, and I object to this document being accepted into evidence because I think that this is in contravention of Rule 85 of the Rules. And as I explained in detail yesterday, I gave the reasons for my objection in general, and this is one of those documents that I feel should not be accepted, where I offered my explanations at the interlocutory appeal pursuant -- against your decision of 18 March of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, but I stand to be corrected, yesterday, in relation to Exhibit 111, the witness was asked whether this document had a receiver -- had sender information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, this witness was asked yesterday whether Exhibit 111 had sender information on it or bore any sign of being sent, meaning that it was received by this witness, and as the -- if I remember correctly, the outcome was that this initial Exhibit 111, that the answer was that there are no sender or receiver signs on it, so that it was possible to draw the inference that the document did not even reach this witness's office. I stand to be corrected on this. I believe that the Prosecution has now shown, by showing this document to the witness and getting the answers from the witness, that the document was signed, that the document was received, and was even processed; so I believe that with this document, I could refresh the witness's recollection about the fact that a proposal had not only been drafted, but even sent to the General Staff Administration for Personnel, was on that basis even processed by this witness. I think this is a lot of new information which, due to the fact that the witness has seen it, was signed, was addressed in the receiver field to his unit, I think based on this new document, I've really refreshed the witness's memory and I've received completely different answers now, and therefore I believe I have refreshed the witness's recollection successfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, just for clarification, could you please explain to us what is the difference between Exhibit 111 and the document we have in front of us? In other words, what's the difference between the document that was shown yesterday and this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, I can. On Exhibit 111, there indeed, I believe on the second page -- I don't have the exact pages in front of me now -- there are a couple of handwritten remarks, encirclements of persons, and there is one person, I believe it's Mr. Karalic, who is, according to an arrow, drawn on this Exhibit 111, allegedly being moved from one category of incentive to another category of incentive, so the Prosecution accepts that this is indeed a working version. On this document, we can clearly see there are no arrows any longer. It is a final version which is obviously signed and thereby authorised by Commander Mahmuljin and sent in this form to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that Exhibit 111 was a draft version of the document that we now have in front of us, which was the final version?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has checked, for example, this arrow, the handwritten arrow, and it looks like that the proposal to move Mr. Karalic from one category of incentive to another category of incentive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to testify now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not a response to the question. The question put was: Are you saying this exhibit is a draft version of the document before us? Yes, it is. No, it is not. Now you want to give us reasons why something has been moved from somewhere else. You're beginning to testify, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand. We have compared both documents, and I personally believe that they are the same except for the handwritings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Be short and concise with your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So the answer is this is the -- sorry. 111 was the draft version, or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Was the draft version, which was not signed, which contains handwritings. This one is the typed-out version without further changes. The handwriting is omitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is one difficulty that stands before the Prosecution. That document, 111, had 74 pages. This one has six pages, so it's not the truth. Secondly, we do not accept that this is an identical document, and there are obvious differences there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you stand up, can I ask the parties to address the Chamber on this point: Forget about Exhibit 111. This is a new exhibit in its own right. In terms of the rules of admission of evidence into -- of exhibits into evidence, what is it that makes this document inadmissible? Can the parties address me on that, please. Madam Vidovic, you are objecting. Why is this document inadmissible on its own right, unrelated to Exhibit 111?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object on the basis that this document was not included in the Prosecution 65 ter list, that the document was intended to establish guilt, and on the basis of all the reasons that I went into yesterday extensively. I do not wish to repeat them here and take up your time. They have to do with the interlocutory appeal of the 18th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Because of the decision we took yesterday, I don't think it is necessary to hear you, Mr. Neuner. The decision was that pending that appeal, we will admit. So we will admit this document, pending the outcome of the decision. You may proceed, Mr. Neuner. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit number 1376.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Before we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, can I just -- I was looking for the PT number of the document on the screen. Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Say again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Before we leave this document, could I have the first page being shown again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I just want you to remember again the reference number, 04/15-114, Witness, because I want to move on to the next exhibit, and that's Exhibit 817. You remember this document, Witness? I believe you have testified about it yesterday, that you drafted it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm the author of the document. I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I don't want to get into the detail of whether you're the author or the drafter of it. I just leave it here. I want to put your attention to the first paragraph of it, and it talks, in the last line, about the proposal of the 3rd Corps commander, on which this document is based, and if you look at the reference number here, could you confirm that that number, 04/15-114, is indeed the same reference number as the document which was just admitted a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you look at number 1, can you confirm that indeed the El Mudjahedin Detachment was commended, as proposed by Mr. Mahmuljin in his document on the 10th of November?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that it was not just one detachment that was commended. There were eight more units, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Five other units, if I count correctly. If we could go on to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And it's the third-last person that's mentioned here. Could you confirm that, in fact, Abu El Maali was commended as proposed by Mr. Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You remember a moment ago we spoke about the rules of acknowledgments and incentives in the ARBiH, and I showed that provision and Article 2 of it, that only in exceptional circumstances foreigners could be awarded. Could you explain what the exceptional circumstances were in the case of Mr. Abu El Maali?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. That question should be answered by the party who proposed this gentleman whom I don't know, and this is the first time I hear of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look at Exhibit 111 again, please. And I'm interested, in the English, in page 21; in B/C/S, in page 74. I think in English, we need to scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you look under number 72, please, this is from the proposal, if you could just read that to yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document is the same as the one you saw before. This is page 74, and that one had six pages. This is the document that the witness said yesterday he had never seen before and that it was a draft, and the Prosecutor again wants to show the document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is wrong with showing the document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness said explicitly that this was the draft of the proposal of the 3rd Corps. He said that yesterday, and that he had never seen the document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Well, I would have hoped that the witness would have given me that answer or, let's put it this way, that he, on his own initiative, would have given me an answer. Now, I mean, maybe this refreshes the witness's recollection and he says, "I have seen it," or, "I have not seen it." I think at this point in time it's a little bit premature to suggest to the witness that he hasn't seen it. He could have looked at me and given an answer, "It was like this," or, "It wasn't like this." I don't know. So far, I don't see a reason for the objection. The witness can speak for himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The point is yesterday the witness told you already that he hadn't seen the entire document. This is what Madam Vidovic is saying, to ask him once again and expect him to say, once again, "I haven't seen the document," is to harp on the same question all over again. That's the nub of the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But the witness has said he received the proposal from Mr. Mahmuljin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which is a six-page document and not a 74-page document. If you can show him this paragraph on that document that he received, it would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I can explain that briefly, Your Honour. I can show the six-page document, which has in the second-last line of it, a reference to an attachment, and the attachment is what Your Honour is seeing in front of you, but this is the attachment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it's the attachment, the attachment is what we see in front of us. Let it be attached to PT6290 [Realtime transcript read in error "PT2690"], not Exhibit 111.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has gone to the archives, and if I understand it correctly, in the archive we could find an elaborated version containing some 70 pages which was established was a draft version, and a signed version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, it is not particularly of interest to the Chamber what investigations the Prosecution did. The Chamber is looking at what should be done in court. If you're saying this page is an annex to PT6290, let it come as an annex to PT6290 and not as an annex to Exhibit 111. Exhibit 111 this witness has disavowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I accept that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In now, if he's disavowed that and you're saying that PT6290 does have an annex, an annex which this witness would have received together with PT6290, go to page 74 of that annex, not this annex. Simply do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I don't have that annex --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you don't have it, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: -- produced, so I would then drop --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You better. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to come to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for the record, I see I've been saying "PT6290" and the transcript keeps saying "PT2690." I hope that can be corrected, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So yesterday -- I want to move on. Yesterday, my learned colleague showed you six documents from the 1st and from the 23rd of December, 1995, and you all saw them. And I'm referring here to Exhibits 79, 817, 827, 829 and 1134. And each document contained awards for ARBiH soldiers, and you said yesterday you had drafted each of these documents. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I processed the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to show you another document, which is PT1916/A, and I want to give you a little bit the background to it. The Office of the Prosecutor had filed an RFA, request for assistance in 2002, to the Bosnian authorities, and received this response which you'll see in a moment in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, what is an RFA?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Request for assistance, I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The Prosecutor is testifying, and this way of proceeding can have a significant bearing and influence the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I didn't intend to testify. I just wanted to explain to this witness the background of this document so that he can study it for himself. This is a response. It says here on the top: "Request of the ICTY from The Hague, the response submitted by ..." I just wanted to introduce the document, that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay, the objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, you see this is from the Federation Ministry of Defence, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you could just have a moment to study it, please. If we can scroll it down a little bit so that the witness can read it. Thank you. And in English as well. Maybe after a moment if we could flip the English page, because I believe the Judges have read. Thank you. If you could maybe now also flip the B/C/S page for a second. So I believe you have read it. I'm interested in not necessarily the letter. This is just the background. I'm interested in the table which is attached to that letter here from the Ministry of Defence. If you could go to the next page, please. We see here there are some tables and -- sorry, it's actually the following page in B/C/S. Yeah. If it is easier, I would have also a handout for you, because I see it's relatively small. If I could ask the usher just so that the witness can properly read it. And this can be shown to the Defence, please, first. Yes. If you please look at the other page which is below, yeah, the one with the smaller table -- the second page, yes. No, it's actually -- yeah, it's this one, exactly. And maybe since the witness has it, could we enlarge a little bit on the English table. I think the B/C/S table is fine as it is. On the English table, could it be enlarged, or is it not possible? I see it cannot be fully seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Mr. Neuner. Is what we see on the English the exact same thing as what we've just seen on the B/C/S? It doesn't look like those two look alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Because we are pressed for time, we couldn't translate the names, but I'm only interested, for the time being, in the columns. I want the witness to explain to us a little bit the document, because he has worked in that section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the document please be enlarged slightly more, if it's possible. If it's not, we'll order double-lens spectacles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I foresaw that situation, but -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you could just look at the table for a second, and we see here we have in the second column the last name. Can you follow? Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And, for example, in the sixth column, we have the corps, the unit in the seventh column. Could you tell me, in the list which you have in front of you, which unit was -- is mentioned here all the time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Prosecutor, I don't want to comment on other people's documents, since I know nothing of them. If it was a document of mine, then I would comment upon each and every one of them. This is -- this was also the first time I saw some of the documents that were made in 2002, while I was already retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand. I just selected this document for you because I believe that it relates to -- it's a statistic which relates to your office. If you could just for one second look at the last column of the document, which says: "Order number" here; is that correct? Could you look at the last column, please? And we see here, under the "Order number," "8/2" at the beginning in each entry. Can you follow me?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And am I correct in that you testified yesterday that "8" is the Administration for Personnel in the General Staff, the number 8?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And "8/2" is, in fact, your section, the Section for Medals and Awards and Incentives within that administration, is it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So am I correct in concluding that the documents listed in the last column, they all refer to documents issued by your unit?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if this is all accurate. I can't know that, because I didn't make this document. That's why I can't give you a yes-or-no answer. You're asking me something that took place 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand that, but isn't it that all documents which were issued by -- or which had the reference number 8/2 were documents produced in your section?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They have a reference number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And if you look for a moment to the ninth column, which is called "Proposal number," do you find here the proposal number in the first line 04/15-114? Do you find that number?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Isn't that the document you have just seen a moment ago from the 10th of November, the proposal by Mr. -- signed by Mr. Mahmuljin? You remember, I asked you to memorise the number.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And if you look in the column left to that number, you see, indeed, the date of the proposal, the 10th of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And if you look to the seventh column, which is entitled "Unit," "VJ" in your language --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: -- do you see that the proposal relates to the [indiscernible] El Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So if we go back to the very last column, is it not that all that is done here on the table is the documents which were discussed yesterday and today, they were just listed here by the Ministry of Defence, and as you can see in the last column, this is just the reference number given by your office to that particular document which awarded that person?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there's nothing controversial there. We discussed this yesterday in relation to the documents. We have two dates, the 11th and 3rd of December --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure if the 11th refers to November.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of 1995. That was at the time when this detachment was supposed to be disbanded, and it was being worked on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the dates, because the interpreters couldn't get the dates.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dates are the months of November and December of 1995. So that was toward the end of the year, on the eve of, or during the signing of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can the witness repeat his answer in the entirety, because one sentence which had to do with the disbandment was not entered into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. All these documents were produced in the months of November and December of 1995. It was on the eve of the signing of the Dayton Accords or thereafter, which meant that this was done on the dictate of the political circles where the intention was to have these men disarmed and to have the matter of this unit resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where do you get it, that it was done under the dictate of the political circles, and what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer that, although I partly answered that yesterday. I was a member of the SDA party and a member of the town board of Sarajevo. I knew what was going on. We had knowledge about this unit, and Mr. Izetbegovic was telling us what was supposed to be done for the Dayton Accords. To solve this matter, he summoned Mr. Vranj, and Mr. Vranj told me in turn that Mr. Izetbegovic had told him that these people should be given these awards and that the intention was to have this unit disbanded, so that we avert any possible conflicts with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And by "Mr. Izetbegovic," you mean the president of the Presidency of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I would just like to ask that this document is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, because I understand that you said you were under pressure of time, Mr. Neuner, but in the transcript you have referred to a number of particulars that are in these columns, which are not there in the English version, and for our sake if you can make sure and agree with the opposite side that at least to what you had referred to in evidence is mentioned in the various columns.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We will produce -- sorry. We will produce a fully-fledged translation of that table, containing all the names and all the data, so that will then be uploaded to e-court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have two objections against the admission of this document into evidence. First of all, it is quite apparent that the witness commented only upon the table and only that part of the document can be tendered into evidence. The witness clearly said that he had no knowledge of this letter. I would like to draw Their Honours attention to a practice adopted by the Prosecution which is highly unfair. The letter by the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was signed by none other than Mr. Ferid Buljubasic, a witness for the Prosecution who testified a while ago. This document dates from 2002, and is a document that the Prosecution had in their possession under a different number. However, Your Honours, they did not show the letter to Mr. Ferid Buljubasic, or perhaps they had and we're not aware of the comment he may have made, but they did not lead the document during his testimony. What they what want to do now is to have this document introduced through the back door and through a witness who has no knowledge about the document. Therefore, first of all, I object to the admission of this document into evidence. What is possible, that this document is admitted into evidence to the extent and only with regard to the page that the witness commented on. Now, I want to say that this document that the Prosecutor marked P1916/A was also not on the 65 ter list. It was also intended to be used to establish the guilt of the accused, which means that it is applied in contravention of Rule 85 of the Rules. Let me not go again into that matter. It has to do with the interlocutory appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I just answer briefly, because there is one thing which is not correctly presented here. This document was, since the very beginning of this trial, on the Prosecution's 65 ter list. It is PT1916, so it was available to the Defence. And this document is an excerpt out of this PT1916, and the Prosecution has therefore, since it's only an excerpt, introduced this today and a few days before to the Defence under the name PT1916/A. That's the established practice which was used by the Prosecution throughout this trial, if only excerpts from greater or larger portions are submitted. So also the translation of this document has been communicated in advance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you take your seat, please, Madam Vidovic, and let him finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Other than that, the Prosecution believes that the reasons brought forward by my learned colleague go to the weight this Chamber may address to that document, and the Prosecution has chosen this witness to comment upon it because he was, in fact, the chief of the section for medals and awards, and we therefore believe that this witness is better suited to comment upon a list, listing his own documents which he has, as he testified yesterday and today, drafted. Then Mr. Ferid Buljubasic, who as Your Honours can see according to the signature, was at the time deputy minister and in that form had only -- as one of his several tasks the task to forward letters and correspondence to the ICTY. We believe that this witness is better suited to comment upon documents which he, even in 1995, has drafted. Mr. Buljubasic did not draft a single document which was discussed yesterday and today in the year 1995. He only was, in 2002, in the position as deputy minister to forward correspondence to the ICTY. So we believe this witness is better suited to comment upon this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is up to you to assess whether it is preferable for a witness, who has never seen a letter -- this letter, to comment on it or to show it to the author, Mr. Ferid Buljubasic, who drafted this letter and who could testify on it. What I would like to stress, once again, is that this is not the same document as P1916, it is not the same document. By just glancing at the first page, you can see that it's not the same document, and my objection remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Two issues are not determined here. The parties are in dispute about them: One, whether PT1916/A is the same as PT1916, and also the question whether it was on the 65 ter list and therefore subject of the pending appeal or not. To the extent that there are those two issues outstanding, the document will be marked for identification, and may it please be given an exhibit number, pending the resolution of those two disputes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the documents will become Exhibit number 1377, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Will that be a convenient time, Mr. Neuner?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Absolutely convenient time. Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at -- what, is this the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. Quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Quarter to 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, you said you have no further questions. Any re-examination, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I actually would have a clarification with regard to the two open points, and I tried to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you did send the message, but, sorry, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. I hope this takes a very short time. I have already given the document to my learned colleague, and I have three other documents for the Bench, just to clarify the two contentious issues which Your Honours have raised before the break. If I could ask the usher, please. What Your Honours have in front of you are two things. The first two pages is an excerpt of the exhibit list. You will remember I had asked that PT1916/A should be introduced into evidence, and what you find here in the second row is the entire exhibit as it was on the exhibit list -- 65 ter exhibit list of the Prosecution on the 31st of October, 2006. If you look here at the B/C/S ERN range, it's the second-last column in the second row, Your Honour, you'll see it's the range is 0217-1248 to 0217-1260. And if you go to the next page, Your Honour, you'll find a printout of the entire range, I believe some 13 pages, and if you, in this printout of the entire range, go to the fifth page with the ERN 0217-1252, you'll find the excerpt of -- you'll find, first of all, the letter and the excerpt which I have shown a moment ago. You'll find here the two-page letter of Mr. Buljubasic, followed by a list -- two lists, actually, and these are the two lists which I have shown. And the other documents which follow thereafter are, indeed, also exhibits by now which have been tendered under different numbers and which were discussed yesterday and today by my learned colleague and myself with this witness. But with my last application, I was just trying to get the letter and these two tables into evidence. I hope this explains everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, any response?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do have a response. I still consider these documents to be different, because obviously this document has -- contained far more -- many more communications, and if the Prosecutor wanted to show the witness this table, which is what he wanted to do, I don't see any reason why he could not use the P1916 document and rather chose to pick out from this entire communication, and I cannot comment on the rest of the document at this point, Your Honour, but obviously he's singled out this letter, the letter from Mr. Buljubasic, who at this time was the Chef de Cabinet of General Delic and who has already testified here, and has several pages, so it cannot be claimed that this is the same document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, hasn't it been done right through this trial that parties have come with voluminous documents, but have referred to just parts of them, and in fact we have a guideline that says that in that event the Chamber will admit just the pages that are referred to or something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's exactly what I was pointing out. There was no reason then to use a document which was not on the list and the document P1916/A was not on the list, so there was not a single reason why he shouldn't use this document, which was on the list and which then he could use, in part, the tables that he used, and then to propose that these tables be entered into evidence. The problem here is that the Prosecutor wants this letter also to be entered into evidence, and the witness did not comment -- make any comments on the letter. He did make comments on the table. So I do not have an objection to this part, his using document P1916, which was on the 65 ter list and which contained in it the table, but my objection is to the other part. And on the other hand, Your Honour, had he placed this document on the list for us as document 1916, then I would have prepared differently for this. I really don't know what else there is in this document. That's the problem. So to summarise, I agree completely with you, I have no objections to using that part of the document that the witness did make comments on, but the witness did not comment on the letter. So this was one basis for my objection. The other basis was the fact that P1916/A was not on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. There's something I'm missing here. I understand Mr. Neuner to be saying that these documents that he has just hand out are part of -- wait a minute, that the documents that he used are part of the 65 ter list, Exhibit number 1916, and that entire document, which was voluminous, was disclosed to the Defence and the list was given to the Defence right at the beginning. But from that voluminous document, he took the part that he used today, which is tantamount to having a thick document, but using just part of it. Can you confirm that I am understanding you correctly? Just "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If that is so, then that position differs from your position, where you are saying the document that was shown, that is, 6290, is not part -- is it 6290? No, no. 1916/A is not part of 1916. Your positions are different. You are saying it is not part of 1916, and he says it is part of 1916.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, that is not what I am claiming. I accept that this was part of the document P1916. It is part of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. Let's just stop there, because this is where my confusion is. Now, if you accept that, what is wrong with taking part of -- discussing part of 1916 with the witness, because this is a document that you had notice of through the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what is wrong is that the Prosecutor took a piece of -- a part of this document and put it -- and assigned a different exhibit number to it, and as such it was not on the 65 ter list, because had he done so, then I would have prepared myself differently for today's session, because the problem is not that this document is very voluminous, because -- that is not the crux of the problem. Had he done what he should have, and I still claim that it's not the same document, I would have prepared myself differently. So he could have just taken a portion of the document and use it. This has been done many times until now, so I could propose P1916 and say, for instance, "Could you just take a look at page 15," and only page 15 would then be tendered into evidence. That's not what he did. What he did is he took portions of the document and then assigned new numbers to it, saying that this was P1916/A, and then informed me that he would be using this number. That's one objection. The other one is that this document, the letter that is really in dispute here, he did not show to the witness, his own witness who was in a position to give his own explanation and comment on this letter because he was its author. And, secondly, what I said was this witness did not comment on the letter at all. He only commented on the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand you. Are you using the fact that he did not show it to his own witness as a ground for objection, because I want to believe that it's not for you, nor for anybody, to tell him how to prosecute his case. If he thinks there is a witness that can comment on any document, he can use any witness. That's his right. But I heard him say, if I may respond to the point you're raising on the use of "/A," I heard him say before the break that this is what is being done when you take only a portion out of a document that you have already disclosed through a 65 ter list, you give it the same number, but then you "/A." This is what he said, and I haven't heard you comment on that. In other words, the substantial -- substantive difference would be that he would be arguing that it is not a new number, it is not a new document, it is a part of an existing document. And you're saying because he has given it the same number and just slashed it with an "A," that makes it a different document?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, because in this way he actually made it impossible for me -- or rather he denied me my duty to check this whole document and prepare differently for today. And, Your Honour, with due respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the document, the whole document. Why didn't you go through the whole document, even before he produced 1916/A? The purpose of giving you this 65 ter list and disclosing the documents under Rule 66 is for you to go through the whole documents and prepare. And you can't then say, "I can't use part of the documents that I've handed over to you because you've taken them out."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course I went through all the documents, but not at this point while this witness is testifying, because this is when I should have been told that P1916 would be used, because I'm entitled to prepare for my Defence with this witness. That's one thing. The second thing: What you said, that the Prosecutor cannot be told how to lead his evidence, Your Honour, there is Rule 94, I believe, (H) which makes it incumbent upon the parties to present their cases, and then they cannot turn their backs on the witnesses and present documents after the witness has left. Perhaps he was in a position to give us very relevant information, that earlier witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Vidovic, because of what you said, or through what you said, do you mean to say that when you saw the document 1916/A, you thought that it was a new -- a novel document when you prepared for the testimony of your witness, so you didn't connect this document with the one in the 65 ter list? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, can I just ask you: When were you notified of 1916/A?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I could maybe answer that very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I want to hear from her.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it was yesterday, around 12.30. I will check, but I think it was around 12.30 yesterday. And another thing, Your Honour. This issue has been resolved in our case law, when a document can be used which was not on the 65 ter list. In the Hadzihasanovic case, it was resolved or ruled that such a document has to be presented to the other party at least 24 hours ahead of time. Of course, I'm aware of the fact that this has not been an issue that was resolved in our guidelines, but it is in the practice of this Tribunal that it should be 24 hours ahead of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: First of all, I want to say I'm sorry for the length of this discussion. The Prosecution has checked its e-mail traffic from yesterday, and we have seen that the document -- or the Prosecution's exhibit list was communicated at 2.06 in the afternoon, so before the examination-in-chief started. And we have looked at our -- at the lists relating to Mr. Loncaric which we have sent, and it turns out that we have twice referred to this particular exhibit. We have referred to it under 1916/A, and we have also referred to it as 1916. So we have two rows on the exhibit list which we sent -- communicated before the examination-in-chief started. So we have even referred to the entire exhibit, as well as to the portion of it, so it cannot be claimed that the Prosecution tried to introduce a new portion of it or whatever. Both the excerpt and the entire exhibit have been referred to, and I believe this was all but -- all and fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if that is the case, and I'm sorry that my colleague should point it out in this way, but what he says, that the document P1916 was mentioned, there was no mention of "P" or "A" or "D" or anything. And I asked my Colleague Neuner yesterday, before our session, what this meant, particularly because there are two question marks in front of this document. We've discussed this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I can clarify this very, very briefly. I'm very sorry for this discussion, but it is true I delivered a -- in addition to the e-mail which I sent to my learned colleague, I brought a hard copy to my learned colleague when I entered the courtroom, and my colleague looked at the numbers which I had stated in the 65 ter column, and so to speak reminded me that there is no "P" number or no "D" number mentioned. I then talked to our case manager, Ms. Imamovic-Ivanov, and she reacted immediately and clarified that point. And seven minutes later, I think at 2.22 -- 2.27, I'm just informed, she re-sent the list with adequate "P" numbers in front of it. So the omission that there was no "P" in front of the "1916" was immediately after I was informed by my learned colleague, and rectified by the Prosecution. It was simply an oversight. As I had stated, I made two efforts before, via e-mail and via hard copy when I entered the courtroom, to notify my colleague adequately about the 65 ter list the Prosecution was using. We were then rectifying the omission that there was no "P" in front of it, and this took a few minutes' time, and the document was resent in an adequate manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course I was engaged in the examination of the witness, and it is quite possible I didn't have a chance to look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Look, this has taken too long to discuss, and I would like to suggest a modus operandi and a modus vivendi for the parties for the future. Usually, the one presents a case, either it's a motion or it's an objection, there's a response and there's a reply, and that's the end of the discussion and we get a ruling. Any further discussions can only be with the leave of the Court, and I think we must stick to that practice for the sake of expeditiousness in the future. On this issue, the Chamber decides to admit the document. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to the record, the document is already Exhibit number 1377.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Without the MFI?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. The MFI becomes Exhibit 1377.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have but a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Loncaric, once again. During your testimony yesterday, the Prosecutor put a series of questions to you, suggesting that you did not meet with Delic after his appointment, nor did you have occasion to review the minutes from these meetings. In your evidence, you also told us that you were a member of the town board of the Party of Democratic Action. Can you tell us what the SDA town board was?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town board of the Party of Democratic Action was the party's board for the town of Sarajevo. Every municipality nominated five candidates, and they were members of the board.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the governing body of the ruling party or not?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the governing body of the ruling party in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was that body ever visited by President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was visited by President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I didn't put a single question in my cross-examination about the SDA, about Mr. Izetbegovic, and about the town board to this witness. Therefore, I object against the line of question -- the entire line of questions which was just pursued by my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I ask these questions of the witness in order to establish what the basis of his knowledge of some facts was, and these were facts referred to by the Prosecutor. His question was whether he, the witness, attended meetings, and I want to establish what the basis of his knowledge was, if the knowledge did not come from his attendance at the meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, you can ask questions, but, you see, when you start asking questions by giving a whole speech and introducing issues, like, "During your testimony yesterday, the Prosecutor put a series of questions to you, suggesting that you did not meet with Delic after his appointment, nor did you have occasion to review the minutes from these meetings. In your evidence, you also told us that you were a member of the town board of the Party of Democratic Action... " There's no question. Now, you're bringing in things that he's objecting to. If you want to ask questions about the facts that he raised, ask those questions directly, go straight to your question. And if you want to direct the attention of the witness to a particular topic, say, "I would like to direct your attention to this topic," and then ask your questions. The way you're doing it, it's not it. So to that extent, I'll hold up the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what was the basis of your knowledge of the events you testified about concerning the General Staff and the relations in the General Staff in the course of the summer of 1993? And I'm referring to yesterday's testimony.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis -- or the source of the information was my membership of the town board of the Party of Democratic Action in Sarajevo, which discussed military matters, matters which had to do with the situation in the army. Furthermore, President Izetbegovic and other party members would attend these meetings of the town board and discuss matters and events taking place outside of Sarajevo, and I attended these meetings. Now, when it came to these issues of the General Staff, we, the Patriotic League, met regularly in the Staff of the Supreme Command and discussed various matters which had to do with the current developments and the state of affairs in the Staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 66, lines 20 and 25, the Prosecutor asked you who General Vranj reported to, and General Vranj is your superior. Your answer was: "For the most part, to President Izetbegovic." What I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you referring to yesterday's transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I apologise. That was your yesterday's testimony on page 66, lines 20 and 25. You said there that General Vranj, for the most part, reported to President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will explain what the situation was like. With General Delic being appointed head of the army, General Vranj was automatically appointed the head of the Personnel administration and I was appointed head of the department, so Sulejman Vranj and I were both members of the party, though admittedly General Vranj had more authority and was better acquainted with President Izetbegovic and other members of the SDA party. Therefore, the personnel administration was manned with people from the political circles, so that whatever was topical in political terms could be resolved through administration. Yesterday, the Prosecutor wanted to downplay my role by saying that I was a desk officer and that I wasn't aware of some matters. Well, I have to tell you that I knew some matters better than my superior, because I was present where discussions took place and I took part in these discussions myself. I stated yesterday that I had no military experience at all. My first promotion was in 1994, when I was promoted to the rank of colonel. Then as Sakib Mahmuljin became assistant minister, during his term of office I was promoted to the rank of brigadier and was retired in 2000 with that rank. This meant that after all, I did have a role to play, I did have knowledge, I had the relevant information, and I did make decisions on some matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify the following: Wherein did your authority lie? You said that you held a lower rank, but you did make certain decisions?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained yesterday that I was a member of the SDA town board and that I was on good terms with the leaders of the SDA party, including President Izetbegovic, whom I knew from the electoral campaign and from the time of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I only wanted to ask you to slow down a bit. My question dealt specifically with what you said, that General Vranj was the one who passed information on to President Izetbegovic. Can you explain this a bit?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. If it is the politics that appoints you to a certain post, that it is only normal that you should report back to the politics on what is going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answering my question, you said that you passed information on. Were you, in fact, talking about reporting to President Izetbegovic or only discussing matters with him?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to discussing matters with President Izetbegovic and passing on information to President Izetbegovic from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't think the transcript reflects what you've said. Your Honour, the witness uses a very clear term which is not entered into the transcript. Can you please tell what you said in your last answer? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sulejman Vranj received assignments from President Izetbegovic, processed them, and that, along with the tasks he processed in the Main Staff, he would go back to President Izetbegovic and report to him, convey that information to him, and all this behind the back of General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was this standard procedure, based on your knowledge on how the Main Staff works?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course this was not standard procedure. The normal procedure would have been for General Vranj to send all his proposals to the army commander. However, this did not take place. We worked quite differently. I explained how it went when I talked about citations and incentives. And I want to add something else. When we're referring to my department, the Department for Education, Citation and Decorations, decorations lay within the purview of the Presidency and not within that of General Delic. Now, I wish to explain why it was that my department included that word in its title. Mr. Izetbegovic asked that these matters be included in my department as part of the duties of my department, that the department should process these matters and refer them to the Presidency, because he fully trusted the work of that administration and that particular department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I would have thought that what you told us yesterday about decorations would be different from what you and Vranj report to Izetbegovic behind Mr. Delic's back, because yesterday you said the only reason Mr. Delic didn't sign some of the documents, it was because he would be absent. So if he would have been present, he would have signed. So these are documents that would have gone through him, anyway, but what then you discuss with Izetbegovic behind his back, it's what you do behind his back, whether he's present or not present. Aren't these two different scenarios? Would you agree that these two are different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were two different scenarios, and I'll explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't have to explain. I just wanted to know that they are different. So you can't liken them. I'm just saying this because you said something that decorations are the same thing as what you tell Izetbegovic behind Mr. Delic's back. I thought the one is, so far as I'm concerned, gossip, and the other one is work. Wouldn't you say so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you think that they are different things, no, it's just the decorations and citations that are different, because the citations and incentives were within the purview of the commander and the decorations were within the purview of the president of the Presidency. This is something that I explained yesterday, that we did not actually deal with the matters that had to do with decorations at all. We only dealt with citations and incentives because they were within the competence of the commander. Decorations, which were within the purview of the president, we did not discuss yesterday at all. I only said that they were the highest-level awards and were within the competence of the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that very well. You're introducing something new now. You may continue, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you explain the purview or competence yesterday, and did you explain the difference between decorations, citations and incentives?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who had the competence to award decorations?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president or, actually, Presidency; that is to say the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And who has the competence to sign citations and incentives?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this is something you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm saying the same thing today. I only wanted to explain the worthiness of this department, because they were given, in their name, the decorations to deal with, although they lay within the purview of the Presidency -- of the president of the Presidency and I would approach him on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I want to ask you something else. Yesterday, when talking about the awarding of citations, the Prosecutor asked you whether you, that's to say the administration, consulted with the Military Security Administration concerning the proposed recipients of awards and, in particular, concerning their possible criminal records. My question to you is the following: Who had the competence of vetting or screening the individual who was to receive the award and that individual's possible criminal background?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I gave my answer to the Prosecutor yesterday. The competence and the duty to screen the individual who is proposed for the award lies with the proposing party. It is not regulated anywhere that we should be the ones to double-check the person's background and see whether the person is eligible for the award.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were also questions either from the Prosecutor or the Honourable Chamber regarding the reasons stated for why these proposals were as they were, and you said that these were short statements of reasons where it was mentioned that they had accomplished a certain mission. I would like to ask you this: When speaking of the El Mudjahedin Detachment, do you remember whether such a statement of reasons was given and what it was?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no statement of reasons, I mentioned this yesterday, because it was Mr. Izetbegovic who was most involved in the awarding of citations to them.
